title: Orchestrators, not customers: A new role for European governments in defence – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: A retired Turkish general proposes 'ADIEM' - a model where European governments become orchestrators of a continuous defense-innovation ecosystem rather than slow, sequential buyers, arguing Europe's real defense constraint is speed and fragmentation, not money.

insights.claim: Europe's core defense problem is not funding but that its procurement systems remain slow and fragmented in an era when military technology can change in months rather than decades.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: Investors should discount European defense narratives that focus purely on budget increases and instead track procurement-reform and cycle-time metrics as the real driver of capability delivery.
insights.quote: But money is only part of Europe's defence problems. The main constraint is that its systems remain slow, fragmented and poorly suited to an age when military technology can change in months rather than decades.

insights.claim: Three simultaneous transformations - Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Washington's pivot toward the Indo-Pacific and 'burden shifting' within NATO, and accelerating military technology - are forcing Europe to supply not just more money but a larger share of NATO's actual combat power.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: Signals sustained multi-year demand growth for European-sourced combat capability, not just ammunition stockpiling, relevant to European prime and drone/autonomy suppliers.
insights.locator: Three transformations are hitting the continent at once

themes.theme: Broken procurement model vs. the Ukraine loop

insights.claim: Traditional European defense procurement (requirement defined, specs drawn up, contract awarded, system fielded years later) risks fielding technology that is already obsolete by the time it reaches soldiers.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: Legacy multi-year fixed-spec contracts are structurally exposed to obsolescence risk versus iterative, software-updatable platforms.
insights.quote: Promising technologies can become obsolete or fall by the wayside before they ever reach soldiers.
insights.locator: At present, procurement systems work as follows

insights.claim: Ukraine has demonstrated an alternative model where operational battlefield problems generate ideas that engineers turn into prototypes, soldiers test in combat, manufacturers scale, and battlefield feedback loops into the next iteration - and Europe should make this cycle permanent.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: Companies able to plug into rapid iterate-test-field loops (vs. classic multi-year primes contracts) are better positioned to capture the next wave of European defense-tech spend.
insights.locator: Ukraine has demonstrated a different model

insights.claim: The right measure of defense-industrial success is not the volume of platforms produced but how fast a capability can be imagined, built, tested, industrialized, fielded and adapted again.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: Reframes the KPI investors and policymakers should use to judge European defense-industrial competitiveness away from unit output toward cycle-time.
insights.quote: The real measure of defence-industrial success should not be how many platforms roll off the line, but how fast capability can be imagined, built, tested, industrialised, fielded and adapted again.

insights.claim: Because digital defense capability now depends as much on software and data engineering as on heavy manufacturing, Europe's defense sector is competing directly with commercial tech companies for the same scarce engineering talent.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: Talent-pipeline and compensation competitiveness becomes a leading indicator for which European defense-tech firms can actually scale software-heavy capability.

insights.claim: The proposed 'Adaptive Defence Industrial Ecosystem Management' (ADIEM) model calls for governments to shift from being regulators and buyers to orchestrators linking armed forces, defense and tech companies, start-ups, universities and investors in a continuous loop.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: A governance-model shift like this would favor venture-backed defense start-ups and dual-use tech firms with direct access to military end-users, at the expense of pure prime-contractor intermediation.

insights.claim: The author recommends hybrid procurement: central agencies continue buying major systems while individual military units are allowed to meet urgent combat needs directly, alongside breaking large contracts into smaller incremental-delivery pieces with continuous software updates and open architecture.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: Open-architecture, incremental-delivery contracting favors smaller, modular suppliers over monolithic multi-year platform programs.
insights.locator: Make procurement faster and more flexible

insights.claim: The author calls for dedicated programs to achieve 'affordable mass' - weapon systems effective, cheap and simple enough to buy in large numbers and replace quickly, specifically citing drones, autonomous vehicles, loitering munitions, low-cost ISR and electronic warfare systems.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: Directly names the equipment categories the author expects to see sustained European procurement demand for - a useful screen for defense-tech investment theses.

insights.claim: The author calls for building sovereign digital defense infrastructure - a sovereign defense cloud, secure data architecture, digital twins and common digital standards - as a distinct required investment layer alongside physical hardware.
insights.speaker: Yavuz Türkgenci
insights.so_what: Points to a specific European sovereign-cloud/defense-data infrastructure buildout as an adjacent investable theme to hardware rearmament.
